title: The Horse in Motion
titleOriginal: The Horse in Motion. "Sallie Gardner," owned by Leland Stanford; running at a 1:40 gait over the Palo Alto track, 19th June 1878

source.author: Eadweard Muybridge; animation by Commons user Avelludo (2024) from the Library of Congress scan of the 1878 cabinet card

object.medium: Twelve wet-plate photographs taken by electrically tripped cameras, published as a cabinet card; shown here as a reconstructed silent animation
object.description: On 19 June 1878, at Leland Stanford's stock farm at Palo Alto, Eadweard Muybridge lined up twelve cameras along a track, each with a shutter tripped by a thread the horse broke as it passed. The mare Sallie Gardner, running at about forty kilometres an hour, took the twelve pictures herself in under half a second. Stanford wanted to settle an old argument: does a galloping horse ever have all four feet off the ground? The plates showed that it does, but with the legs gathered under the body, not stretched out fore and aft as painters had always drawn them. Muybridge sold the sequence as a cabinet card and, from 1880, spun the frames on a glass disc in his zoopraxiscope so that audiences could watch the horse run. That projector is a direct ancestor of cinema, and the stop-motion study of movement he began here filled the eleven volumes of Animal Locomotion in 1887. What is shown here is a modern animation of the eleven usable frames of the 1878 card.
facts: The exposures were about a thousandth of a second, far faster than any studio portrait of the day.
Stanford paid for the work; the legend that it settled a $25,000 bet is unproven.
Muybridge's zoopraxiscope projections of 1880 were among the first moving pictures shown to a paying public.
Muybridge had been acquitted of murdering his wife's lover in 1875, three years before this sequence.
